ideas.title: Budget-first company card
ideas.summary: When the company card is swiped, the purchase goes to the budgeting app first. The app approves or declines it against the budget, then the bank pays.

verdicts.note: Card platforms are built for this. Stripe Issuing sends each purchase to our app, which answers yes or no within 2 seconds (Lithic allows 6). The card has to be ours, not their old bank's card.
No new bank needed. The card platform's sponsor bank holds the money and the license; we make the yes or no call.
Ramp, Brex and Divvy sell credit cards. A debit card that stops at the budget line is open ground.
Money comes from a share of card fees plus a monthly plan. Get Stripe's and Lithic's real prices before promising anything.

ideas.next: Try it on DarkDorms first: one company card with one budget rule.

ideas.title: Limits on the whole bank account
ideas.summary: Set limits on one bank account so transfers and bills, not just card swipes, must fit the budget.

verdicts.note: Card swipes are easy to stop. Transfers and checks can only be stopped if the money sits in an account our partner runs, not at Chase or another outside bank.
Holding the business's main account brings more bank rules. Start with card spending, add accounts later.
Relay shows owners like a separate account per purpose. Hard limits on those would set us apart.

ideas.title: Start our own bank?
ideas.summary: Would the app need its own bank to sit between the card and the banking system?

verdicts.note: No. A charter takes 2 to 4 years and $2M to $5M+ (vendor estimate). A sponsor bank gives us the same card rails in weeks.
That money would mean investors or loans. A sponsor bank lets us start debt-free.

ideas.next: Revisit only if the app grows big enough that partner fees hurt.

ideas.title: Envelopes that refill from sales
ideas.summary: Every deposit splits into envelopes (taxes, inventory, payroll, owner pay). The card can only spend what is in the matching envelope.

verdicts.note: Relay sells up to 20 accounts to Profit First fans. Pairing envelopes with declines at the swipe is new.
Makes the tax set-aside automatic, like Penny's 25% rule for DarkDorms.
Envelopes are balances in our app; the yes or no check just reads them.

ideas.next: Make envelopes the heart of the first version.

ideas.title: Over budget? Text the owner
ideas.summary: When a worker's purchase is over budget, the owner gets a text and can say yes or no.

verdicts.note: The card network waits only about 2 seconds, too short for a text. So: decline, text the owner, and a Yes raises the limit so the worker can retry.
Small teams want this. It works like the Yes and No buttons on this island.

ideas.next: Design the decline, text, retry loop.

ideas.title: Built for debt-free owners
ideas.summary: Sell to owners who run their business debt-free (EntreLeadership and Profit First crowds), churches and nonprofits.

verdicts.note: These owners already avoid credit cards, and the big players all push credit.
It's a niche. Test demand with a simple waitlist page before building.

ideas.next: Draft a one-page waitlist site when you're ready.

ideaVerdict.call: Viable as an app on a partner bank, not as a new bank. Start with the budget-first debit card and envelopes.
ideaVerdict.next: Test it debt-free on DarkDorms: ask Stripe for Issuing access for DarkDorms, build one budget rule, and put up a waitlist page.
